question: A 70-year-old male visits his primary care physician because of progressive weight loss. He has a 20-year history of smoking 2 packs of cigarettes a day and was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus 6 years ago. After physical examination, the physician tells the patient he suspects adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas. Which of the following physical examination findings would support the diagnosis:?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas" -> "possible obstruction of the bile duct" -> "enlarged gallbladder" -> "palpable gallbladder" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas" -> "possible metastasis" -> "lymphadenopathy" -> "umbilical lymphadenopathy (Sister Mary Joseph's nodule)" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas" -> "insulin resistance" -> "possible acanthosis nigricans" -> "unclear correlation with pancreatic cancer" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas" -> "possible splenic vein obstruction" -> "splenomegaly" -> "possible but less common finding" -> 65%
CHAIN: "Adenocarcinoma at the head of the pancreas" -> "possible renal artery involvement" -> "renal artery bruits" -> "unclear relevance to pancreatic cancer" -> 60%
analysis: In the context of suspected adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign) is indicative of biliary obstruction, which can occur due to a mass at the head of the pancreas. This finding supports the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. Other options, such as lymphadenopathy of the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph's nodule), acanthosis nigricans, renal artery bruits, and splenomegaly, are less directly associated with pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
